title: On the uniqueness of the strictly convex quadrilateral central configuration with a fixed angle

predicted_errors.error_location: Lemma 2, proof: the four eigenvalues ζ1–ζ4
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: From (18), 2η = S13/r13 = m1m3(δ − r13^{-3}), and R13 = m1m3(δ + 2/r13^3). Hence ζ1 = R13 − 2η = 3 m1 m3 / r13^3, not m1m3/r13^3 as written. The same factor 3 is missing in ζ2, ζ3 and ζ4. (The factor 3 does reappear later in the stated value of a0, so the paper is internally inconsistent.)

predicted_errors.error_location: Lemma 2, proof: expression for a0 = ζ5·ζ6
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Since ζ5, ζ6 are the eigenvalues of the 2×2 block [[R12, 2ηcosθ],[2ηcosθ, R34]], their product is exactly a0 = R12R34 − 4η²cos²θ. The stated 'a0 = 4 r12³ r13⁶ r14⁶ r23⁶ r24⁶ r34³ (R12R34 − 4η² r12³ r34³ cos²θ)' carries spurious factors (an eigenvalue product cannot be rescaled) and the extra r12³r34³ inside the bracket is wrong. Moreover, the correct computation gives R12R34 − 4η²cos²θ = 3 m1m2m3m4 (1 + δ(r12³+r34³)) / (r12³ r34³), so the final stated value 'a0 = 3m1m2m3m4(1+(r12³+r34³)δ)' is also missing the 1/(r12³r34³) factor and is inconsistent with the prefactor written just above.

predicted_errors.error_location: Lemma 2, proof: the substitution cos θ = −S12/(2η r34) = r12(R12 − 3/r12³)/(2η r34)
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: S12 = m1m2 r12(δ − r12^{-3}) = r12 (R12 − 3 m1 m2 / r12³). Hence −S12/(2η r34) = − r12 (R12 − 3 m1m2/r12³)/(2η r34): the displayed equality has the wrong sign and omits the mass factor m1m2 (so the bracket R12 − 3/r12³ is even dimensionally inhomogeneous). The same two defects appear in the companion formula for S34.

For a strictly convex quadrilateral the quantity defined by (10) can be obtuse. Counterexample: P1=(0,0), P2=(2,0), P3=(2.2,2), P4=(2.21,2.5) is strictly convex (all consecutive cross products positive) and (10) gives cos θ = (r24²+r13²−r23²−r14²)/(2 r12 r34) ≈ −0.022, i.e. θ ≈ 91°. Consequently the restriction θ ∈ [0,π/2] is not justified, Lemma 3 (which only treats cos θ > 0 and cos θ = 0) does not cover all strictly convex quadrilaterals, and Theorem 1 as stated ('a given angle of one pair of opposite sides') is broader than what is proved.
D1 = {(r14,r23) ∈ (R+)² : 0 ≤ r14² + r23² ≤ 1/2} is a quarter disk of radius √(1/2) = 1/√2, not 'a quarter of a disk with radius 1/2' as asserted.

predicted_errors.error_location: Lemma 3, fibration p : M0+ → D ('v1 and w1 are determined uniquely by (22)')
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Equations (22) determine v1² and w1², hence v1 ≥ 0 is unique but w1 = r12 − r34 is determined only up to sign; generically the fiber of p consists of two points (r12,r34) and (r34,r12), not 'a point'. The authors simply assume 'without loss of generality w1 ≤ 0', which discards half of M0+ and is not a legitimate normalization (the two choices give genuinely different labelled configurations). The Euler-characteristic computation therefore rests on an unjustified step.

predicted_errors.error_location: Lemma 3, definition of the ellipsoid E^5(1)
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The mutual-distance vector has six components, so the 5-dimensional ellipsoid Σ_{i<j} m_i m_j r_ij² = 1 lives in R^6, not in R^5 as written ('E^5(1) = {r ∈ R^5 | ...}'). As stated, the set is 4-dimensional and cannot be homeomorphic to S^5(1) ⊂ R^6.

predicted_errors.error_location: Lemma 3, case cos θ = 0 (definitions of H, H1, H2)
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: H is defined in the variables (r12, r34), yet the text says 'Now fix a point (r14, r23) ∈ H' (should be (r12, r34) ∈ H). Likewise H1 is a set of pairs (r14, r23) but is described as 'a contractible quarter of a circle ... in the 2-dimension (r12, r34)-plane'. The variable labels contradict the definitions.

Only three steps (i), (ii), (iii) are listed, but the following paragraph states 'replacing the Cayley-Menger determinant constraints with more simple ones can significantly simplify the calculations in (iii), (iv) and (v)'. Steps (iv) and (v) are referenced but never given.

F4(r) = C(r)A(r) is not a polynomial identity in r for fixed θ; it only holds on the realizable set. Explicit check: starting from the unit square (r12=r34=r14=r23=1, r13=r24=√2, θ=0) and varying only r12 → 1+t, one gets F4 = 16t − 8t³ − 2t⁴ while C·A = 16t − 8t³, so F4 − C·A = −2t⁴ ≠ 0. Moreover the two displayed expressions for A(r) in (14) are not equal: their difference is exactly −2 r24² C(r). Since Lemma 1 differentiates (11) ('∇F4 = ∇C·A + C∇A'), an identity valid in a neighbourhood is required; as written the derivation is invalid. In addition, the proof of Proposition 2 is circular: it first assumes C(r)=0 and substitutes (12) into F4, yet the resulting expression (13) still contains the factor C(r).

predicted_errors.error_location: Section 2.2, text after the definition of C̃
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: 'we can easily check that the collinear and the strictly concave configurations are not in this set' is false. Any planar quadrilateral (convex, concave, or collinear) satisfies r13²+r24²−r14²−r23² = 2(P1−P2)·(P4−P3), hence satisfies C(r)=0 for the corresponding θ. E.g. P1=(0,0), P2=(1,0), P3=(0.5,1), P4=(0.4,0.3) is strictly concave (P4 inside the triangle) and satisfies C(r)=0 with θ ≈ 82° ∈ [0,π/2]; a collinear arrangement P1=(0,0), P2=(3,0), P3=(2,0), P4=(1,0) satisfies C(r)=0 with θ=0.

predicted_errors.error_location: Introduction, paragraph on the Perpendicular Bisector Theorem
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: 'there is no 3-body collinearity in a planar 4-body case and no (n−1)-body collinearity in a planar n-body central configuration' — the second assertion is an unsupported generalization. The Perpendicular Bisector Theorem of [22] yields the strict convexity statement for four bodies; no result excluding (n−1) collinear bodies in a general planar n-body central configuration is known or cited.

predicted_errors.error_location: Abstract ('considered by Simó and Yoccoz in the 1980s')
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The cited work of Simó, [31] 'Relative equilibrium solutions in the four-body problem', Celestial Mech. 18 (1978), dates from the 1970s, not the 1980s; only Yoccoz's unpublished note [38] is from 1986. The dating in the abstract conflicts with the reference list.

The uniqueness conclusion ('U has at most one critical point restricted on C') is deduced from Proposition 3 and Lemma 2 only. Lemma 2 merely says any critical point is a non-degenerate minimum; the uniqueness statement requires Lemma 4 (the Morse-theoretic count α0 = χ(M+) = 1), which is never invoked. The logical chain as written is incomplete.
